title: How To Watch FIDE World Championship 2026 Game 1
summary:
The 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship between defending World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju and Challenger Javokhir Sindarov begins on Tuesday, November 24, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET (local time in Geneva) / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Sindarov will have the white pieces in game one and therefore make the first move of the match. Be sure to tune in to check out the action!

How to Watch the 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship Game 1 Live

Our commentary team features GMs Judit Polgar and David Howell. You can watch the 2026 FIDE World Championship live on Chess.com/TV and on our Chess Twitch and YouTube channels.

Match score

Name | | Rating | 01 | 02 | 03 | 04 | 05 | 06 | 07 | 08 | 09 | 10 | 11 | 12 | 13 | 14 | Score

Gukesh Dommaraju | | 2710 | . | .. | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | . | .

The 2026 Salesforce FIDE World Championship in Geneva, Switzerland decides the next world champion. Uzbek Challenger Javokhir Sindarov Indian Defending Champion plays Gukesh Dommaraju in a 14-game match, with the winner the first to 7.5 points. The players have two hours for 40 moves, then 30 minutes to the end of the game, with 30 seconds added each move from move 41 onward. The prize fund is $2,500,000, with $200,000 for a win and the remaining money split equally. If tied 7-7, a playoff will take place, starting with four games of 15+10 rapid chess.

title: 🏆 Lagno Clinches WR Women's Chess Tour Grand Final, Yip Wins Rapid Portion
summary:
GM Kateryna Lagno won the WR Women's Chess Tour - Grand Final 2026 on Monday after finishing second in both the rapid and blitz portions, clinching the inaugural title in the Semifinals. GM Anna Muzychuk won the blitz portion on Sunday, while IM Carissa Yip won the rapid portion on Monday.

Rapid Bracket

Image: Courtesy of WR Chess.

Players earned up to 10 points in each of the two tournaments on Sunday and Monday. When Anna Muzychuk lost the semifinal match to Yip in the rapid portion, it meant that Lagno had already secured the overall title even by finishing second on both days.

Rank | Player | Rapid Pts | Blitz Pts | Total

1 | Kateryna Lagno | 8 | 8 | 16

2 | Anna Muzychuk | 5 | 10 | 15

3 | Carissa Yip | 10 | 2 | 12

4 (tie) | Mariya Muzychuk | 5 | 2 | 7

4 (tie) | Zhu Jiner | 2 | 5 | 7

4 (tie) | Leya Garifullina | 2 | 5 | 7

7 (tie) | Mai Narva | 2 | 2 | 4

7 (tie) | Vaishali Rameshbabu | 2 | 2 | 4

You can see the prize breakdown of the $40,000 below. Curiously, Anna Muzychuk earned the largest share of the prize fund, $9,500, while Lagno made $8,000.

Quarterfinals: Yip, Anna Muzychuk, Mariya Muzychuk, Lagno Advance

In the Quarterfinals, Yip overcame the top seed GM Zhu Jiner 2-1 in armageddon, Anna Muzychuk beat IM Mai Narva 1.5-0.5, GM Mariya Muzychuk beat GM Vaishali Rameshbabu 1.5-0.5, and Lagno beat IM Leya Garifullina 2-1 in armageddon.

The playing hall. Photo: Lennart Ootes/WR Chess.

Yip and Zhu traded wins in two rapid games, but the American came out on top with the black pieces in armageddon. Zhu was winning, with two knights for a rook and a hopelessly weak enemy king, but couldn't find a knockout blow with one minute on the clock.

Circling back to the first game, though, Yip won a piece on move 12 by forking a piece. The game lasted longer, but it was over. Remember! L.P.D.O.: Loose Pieces Drop Off.

The game bears a striking resemblance to a 12-move loss by World Champion Anatoly Karpov to GM Larry Christiansen. In both cases, the queen creates a fork from the first rank and a knight hangs on the rim of the board. Knights on the rim are dim, they say.

Against Narva, Muzychuk won the second game—and therefore the match—with a temporary bishop sacrifice. It's a funny coincidence, because she lost a game to Lagno the previous day to another Bxh6 piece sacrifice as well.

Mariya Muzychuk defeated Vaishali in a rook endgame in game two, while Lagno's match went to armageddon after two draws, even if she had serious winning chances in both of them. With Lagno under 10 seconds and Garifullina under a minute, either player could have won the nervy armageddon tiebreak after move 50. Ultimately, Lagno won a rook.

That was only the first of two armageddon games Lagno would play on Monday.

Semifinals: Lagno Clinches, Advances With Yip

In the Semifinals, we saw Yip edge out Anna Muzychuk and Lagno defeat Mariya Muzychuk in armageddon.

After a solid draw in game one, Yip won the second game after Anna Muzychuk made an innocent-looking, yet decisive, trade of bishop for knight. Her remaining minor piece, the knight, turned out to be extremely unstable.

Lagno's armageddon game against Mariya Muzychuk was very complicated, but the critical moment came on move 32. For better or worse, White had to prevent the f5 pawn break, even if the resulting position is objectively equal. In the game, Lagno got a decisive initiative.

Final: Yip Wins Rapid Tournament

As GM Elisabeth Paehtz predicted, Yip won the first game of the Final and drew the second to take the match. Paehtz's rationale was that (a) Yip is significantly younger than her opponent and (b) has had a shorter event, since she was knocked out in her first match on Sunday.

In the middlegame, Yip won a pawn, and then went on to convert it in a highly tactical manner, gaining three pawns for the exchange and managing to win without promoting even one of them.

That concludes the WR Women's Chess Tour for this year. We hope you enjoyed the show!

How to watch?

You can watch the event on the WR YouTube channel. The games can also be followed from our Events Page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM Elisabeth Paehtz.

The WR Women's Chess Tour - Grand Final 2026, held in Stuttgart, Germany on November 22 and 23, was the final event of the inaugural tournament series. The top eight qualifiers from the tour played in two single-elimination knockouts, one blitz tournament (3+2 time control) followed by a rapid one (15+10). The overall Grand Final winner was the player with the most combined points from the blitz and rapid tournaments. The prize fund was $40,000, with $7,000 for first place per event.

title: Vishy Anand's Gukesh-Sindarov World Championship Predictions
summary:
We caught up with five-time World Champion Viswanathan Anand ahead of the 2026 World Chess Championship match between reigning World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju and challenger GM Javokhir Sindarov. With Sindarov coming off a spectacular Candidates victory and Gukesh preparing to defend his title, the clash between the two young stars promises an intriguing battle of preparation, form, and nerves.

Anand reflected on why he had picked Sindarov as a Candidates favorite, what makes the challenger so dangerous, and how Gukesh's experience against GM Ding Liren could prove valuable. He also discussed the challenges facing both teams, the psychological significance of the first decisive result, and why recent form can be deceptive. And when asked to put a number on Gukesh's chances, Anand offered a fascinating assessment of just how evenly matched the two players are.

You can watch the interview with CM Tickoo Sahil below:

And we've also transcribed Anand's answers:

Q: When Sindarov won the Candidates, what was your first reaction to him becoming Gukesh's challenger?

[00:33] Anand: I was very happy. I thought this is one of the great matchups we could have had. There were other options which were interesting for other reasons, but I thought both of them... at that point both were still under 20. And potentially a very exciting, very combative match. I thought, "This is a cracker of a match. It should be really good."

[00:56] Q: Was it kind of expected for you that Sindarov was a strong candidate, or were you a bit surprised by how well he played at the Candidates?

[01:02] Anand: I wasn't surprised. I rarely make these predictions; I tend to waffle. But this time I thought, okay, I will pick Sindarov, because I was very impressed by his attitude to danger in the GCL last year in Mumbai. He'd been a teammate, so I saw that close up. So I thought, you have to pick him. I picked Fabi and him, like one old horse and one young horse, kind of thing. And it worked out. Would I have predicted the score and the way he won it? No. It was even more spectacular to watch it unfold, to watch him beat everyone round after round. He caught Fabi in preparation, he caught Hikaru. Literally every single player he caught in some amazing struggle, and he even spoiled a couple of winning positions, so his score could have been even higher, if that's believable. That impression was very strong, and of course I didn't predict that.

Javokhir Sindarov lifts his trophy. Anish Giri took silver, and Fabiano Caruana bronze. Photo: Michal Walusza/FIDE.

[01:58] Q: And what makes Sindarov particularly dangerous in a match situation versus Gukesh?

[02:03] Anand: I think it's this general ease of coming to the board and starting stuff. In a sense that's how he came to Cyprus. There's no way he knew it was going to turn out like this, but he came in the right shape, ready to deal with what happened, and sometimes the upside is huge. I think the greatest danger with Sindarov, from the opponent's perspective, is simply that it can happen. He can just play at a very high level and be in great form. We've seen that in a couple of places, but strongly there, and the rest of the year he's been very stable. If you look at the GCT, he's had sometimes a setback or two, but then he recovers, broadly finishes well, and everywhere he is playing excellently against the top players. So he's in good form generally, and he seems to be happy with life: traveling around, watching football matches, whatever. He seems to be enjoying himself. That's a Zen kind of state to be in.

He seems to be enjoying himself. That's a Zen kind of state to be in.

—Viswanathan Anand on Javokhir Sindarov

[02:58] Q: Indeed, sir. And I think one difference between Gukesh and Sindarov is that Gukesh has obviously gone through one world championship cycle; he's won it before. How valuable is that experience going into his second world championship match?

[03:11] Anand: I think the difference between one and zero is very high. For Gukesh it's definitely a help that he has gone through it once. He can borrow a few things from it. Having said that, these things can influence your form, but mostly your form is how you turn up, and the attitude. This is difficult to fake. It has to happen by itself, and somehow the elements have to fall into place themselves. But for Gukesh it will definitely help, knowing, "Wait, I faced this situation before." Actually, in the Ding match he faced almost everything. He was in the lead, he was behind, kind of everything. It'll help. Definitely, I would rather have played one than zero.

Photo: Gukesh/Instagram.

[03:47] Q: Last time we expected Gukesh to dominate the world championship match, but in the end it was very close. We thought Ding was not in great form. So how much should we read into form going into a world championship?

[03:57] Anand: Form is a very helpful indicator, because sometimes it might just indicate strength. We forget that. We think everything is momentum-driven, but sometimes it may simply indicate that someone is very, very strong. Having said that, we have seen Sindarov at his best, and we have seen Gukesh at his best. Sindarov's form can come to an end. Gukesh's current form can come to an end. Never forget that. And these things are always in your control a little bit. When you're in bad shape, you focus on doing one thing better, then you focus on doing another thing better, and suddenly, you know, the end of the tunnel comes. So you have to have that attitude. Everything goes in a cycle. Ding was not in good shape generally. Also, he was kind of frustrated with life; he's spoken about this. But he turned up and played a great match, with big swings, so you can see he struggled with some things there.

I think in Gukesh there's nothing special. I think he's simply dealing with the pressure and responsibility of being world champion. Maybe the expectations were misaligned and so on. But he is capable of... well, we know what he's capable of. I think he just has to try and get there and play in good shape.

[05:04] Q: Sir, for Gukesh's team, what is the biggest challenge in preparing for Sindarov, and vice versa for Sindarov's team?

[05:11] Anand: Both teams will struggle to predict what the other side is going to do, because both of them clearly will prepare surprises and try to be unpredictable. Still, there's only so far into the other's territory you can go. So they will spend some effort. But I think for Gukesh's team, the focus should be that he's in a shape to play well, pose problems, and feel happy after every game. He should come back thinking, "Oh, that was a good game I played. Now I can do even better." For Sindarov: how do you maintain this form? How do you build on it? I think that will be the challenge for Sindarov's team.

Gukesh 🤝 Sindarov – the first handshake ahead of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026! 📍 Geneva, Switzerland 🇨🇭 🗓 Games: November 24 – December 12, 2026 #GukeshSindarov https://t.co/qGEbbLlegc

— International Chess Federation (@FIDE_chess) November 21, 2026

[05:49] Q: The world championship gives the players a lot of time to prepare, and preparation is a major part of it. You've gone through this cycle multiple times and come out victorious. How important is the preparation for the match itself? And between two players who are youngsters, as you mentioned, 20 years old, is that going to be the defining factor, or do you think something else could be?

[06:07] Anand: Look, it's great to be young. It's great to be 20. Energy levels are not going to be a problem for either of them. All that's going to be very good, but a match is draining even for 20-year-olds. Yes, it'll be challenging. We know the developments in chess, the trends; they'll have to work a lot, a lot of mastering of new concepts, new ideas that keep circulating. It takes time to get familiar with the details, but all things equal, I'd rather be 20!

It takes time to get familiar with the details, but all things equal, I'd rather be 20!

—Viswanathan Anand

[06:35] Q: Fair enough, sir. I think the match is quite interesting because in general both players want to avoid a loss. What do you think happens psychologically after we have the first decisive result in a world championship game? And if Gukesh was on either side, whether it's a win or a loss, what would you advise him in that case?

[06:53] Anand: The first decisive game, well, it's first blood, right? Both sides suddenly wake up. Until you get to Geneva, you're in a slightly dream-like state where there's a big match happening and you have to play well, but you're not always fully awake. It sounds strange, but having had something in front of you for so long, it's very difficult to... whereas if I'm told tomorrow that in one week something is starting, you'll get pumped up much faster. Your adrenaline will jump up much faster. But if you're told some months ago, you kind of lose track of what's happening. After the first decisive result, everybody wakes up: every team member on both sides, the public, everyone wakes up.

After the first decisive result, everybody wakes up.

—Viswanathan Anand

The plus side for the player taking the lead, of course, is that if they're able to keep the right attitude, which is "I should play exactly like I played before, but I have something in the bank to compensate for anything that goes wrong," then that is great freedom. And the pressure is on my opponent, so you can enjoy that situation.

On the other side of it, you think, "My opponent now desperately wants to lower their risk. I can feel it." Sometimes these things happen gradually: one player is slowly withdrawing from risk and the other is... and you just think, "There are seven games left. I need to be calm. I need to start pushing in every game, but gradually, and not do anything silly." That can also be a very liberating attitude. The few times I've been behind, it frees you too. You find yourself able to push further because you understand the score is pushing you. For the player who falls behind that's helpful, but again, it's just as important how your attitude is after taking the lead or falling behind as it was before.

[08:50] Q: Do you think it's different depending on how quickly that first decisive result comes? How is that psychologically different for a player?

[08:56] Anand: Well, if it happens towards the end of the match, the side that's behind is more desperate, and the other side knows there's only very little left in the runway before you hit the end. In the beginning of the match, neither side needs to deal with anything immediately, but you understand, "Now I'm going to have to sit with the lead for 10 to 12 days," not just one or two days. So it's not only enough for me to have a good attitude for the next game; I'll have to keep this good attitude for the next so many games. And the same thing for the other side: I'll have to calmly put pressure on game after game and not lose my belief. So whatever you do, you have to think, "How do I maintain this?" It's more endurance: how do I maintain this for the next 10 days or 20 days, or whatever is left.

[09:44] Q: If Gukesh could take one lesson away from his first world championship match versus Ding, what could that be, that he could apply to get better results?

[09:52] Anand: I think he should just remember what it took, how he felt when he had the highs, and try to remember how it came together.

[10:01] Q: The final question in this segment, the big one: your prediction on who could win, and in terms of Gukesh, what percentage chance would you give him of winning the championship match?

[10:10] Anand: I think they both have comparable strength. Not comparable form, right, but comparable strength. So the percentage is probably going to be very close; 50-50 roughly. But these things don't matter. I'm much more curious to see who'll get that first win, who

title: World Championship matches: Highlights from 140 years of history
summary:
World Championship matches make chess history. Some games are remembered for their beauty, others for dramatic twists, spectacular blunders or their historical significance. As the duel between world champion Gukesh Dommaraju and challenger Javokhir Sindarov gets under way - the 44th World Championship match in the 140-year history of the competition - we look back at 20 remarkable moments from its history. | Pictured: Boris Spassky (left) and Bobby Fischer during the 1972 World Championship match in Reykjavik | Photo: Icelandic Chess Federation

The following list is merely a selection, a suggestion - after all, over the course of 140 years and 44 World Championship matches (1886–2024), 871 games at classical time controls and 19 rapid games have been played. It begins, however, not with a brilliant game, but with one of the most astonishing blunders in World Championship history.

Before the final game of the match between world champion Wilhelm Steinitz and challenger Mikhail Chigorin, Steinitz led by 9 wins to 8. Here, however, Chigorin is winning, but he played 32.Bb4? and allowed mate in two. Chigorin resigned after 32...Rxh2+. The match was over and Steinitz had defended his title.

In the World Championship match between long-time rivals Dr Emanuel Lasker and Dr Siegbert Tarrasch, defending champion Lasker found himself on the defensive after a poor opening. In this position, Lasker sacrificed a pawn with 14...Ng4!? , which Tarrasch gratefully accepted with 15.Bxg7! Nxf2! 16.Kxf2? Kxg7 17.Nf5+ Kh8 18.Qd4+ f6 19.Qxa7 - although perhaps he should instead have played for the attack with 16.Qd4! Lasker obtained unexpectedly rich compensation for the pawn and outplayed Tarrasch, who, surprised by the sudden turn of events, failed to find a good defence. Lasker won the match convincingly by 10½-5½.

Emanuel Lasker (left) and Siegbert Tarrasch during the 1908 World Championship match | Photo source : L. Hoffer, ed. (1908), The Championship Match: Lasker v. Tarrasch, London: E.A. Michell & Frank Hollings

In his World Championship match against Carl Schlechter, Lasker's title, which he had won by defeating Steinitz in 1894, came under serious threat. After 9 of the 10 games, Lasker trailed 4-5 and absolutely had to win the final game. Yet in the diagrammed position, Schlechter could have forced perpetual check with 39...Qh4+. Instead, he played 39...Qh1+? and allowed the white king to escape. Lasker won the game, the match ended in a 5-5 draw and Lasker remained world champion.

Before his World Championship match against defending champion Capablanca, Alekhine had never beaten him. Yet that is exactly what he managed in the very first game of the match. In the diagrammed position, he won an important pawn with 16...Nxc2! 17.Rxc2 Qxf4 . Capablanca, who had probably underestimated both his opponent and the challenges of such a match, never really found his footing afterwards and lost both the match and his title after 34 games (+6, -3, =25 in favour of Alekhine).

The World Championship match between the Dutchman Max Euwe, an amateur who worked as a teacher, and full-time professional Alekhine also produced a surprise. The most famous game of the match is the so-called "Pearl of Zandvoort", which Euwe won with the attractive knight sacrifice 21.Nxf5! . Euwe won the match 15½-14½ and thus became the fifth world champion in chess history. Two years later, however, he lost the title back to Alekhine in the return match. Alekhine remained world champion until his death in 1946, making him the only one of the 18 world champions so far to have died while holding the title.

Tal played 21...Nf4! , producing one of the most famous sacrifices in chess history. Tal won the World Championship match against Botvinnik 12½-8½ and became the youngest world champion ever at the time. The knight sacrifice for attacking chances and long-term compensation was typical of Tal's sacrificial style, which made him famous. Botvinnik regained the title a year later in the return match.

Mikhail Botvinnik (left) and Mikhail Tal at the 1960 Chess Olympiad in Leipzig | Photo: tournament book

Tigran Petrosian became world champion in 1963 by defeating Botvinnik, and in 1966 he defended his title against Spassky. In the most famous game of the match, Petrosian sacrificed the exchange twice and finally ended the game with the attractive queen sacrifice 30.Qh8+ . The match ended 12½-11½ narrowly in Petrosian's favour, but three years later Spassky took revenge at the second attempt and became the new world champion.

In the first game of the legendary World Championship match in Reykjavik between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer, Fischer captured an undefended pawn in a completely equal position with 29...Bxh2? , almost as if he had failed to see that his bishop would be trapped by 30.g3 . Matters were more complicated than that, but the move is nevertheless regarded as a serious mistake. Fischer did not appear for the second game and lost by forfeit. In the end, he won the match 12½-8½ and became the first non-Soviet world champion since the Second World War.

Fischer captures the poisoned pawn on h2. | Photo: screenshot from film footage of the match

Fischer's victory in game six is regarded as a positional masterpiece. Spassky was far from his best form, but was so impressed that he applauded at the end. With this victory, Fischer took the lead in the match for the first time after starting 0-2.

The World Championship match between world champion Anatoly Karpov and challenger Viktor Korchnoi in Baguio City was a bitter and dirty contest, fought inventively and with numerous psychological tricks by both sides both at the board and away from the board. Karpov represented the Soviet Union, while the Leningrad-born Korchnoi had fled the Soviet Union in 1976 and had since been regarded there as persona non grata. The Soviet political system would have regarded a victory by the dissident as a serious defeat. Karpov took a 5-2 lead in wins, but Korchnoi managed to level the score at 5-5. The match was played to six wins, and in game 32 Karpov finally managed to win and defend his title. In the diagrammed position, he sacrificed a pawn with 25.e5! , after which Black's position quickly collapsed.

Garry Kasparov at his best: after a double-edged pawn sacrifice in the opening, challenger Kasparov comprehensively outplayed world champion Karpov - rarely had Karpov's pieces looked so uncoordinated. With this victory, Kasparov took the lead in the match, which he eventually won 13-11.

The game with which Kasparov became world champion. The first World Championship match between world champion Karpov and challenger Kasparov was stopped when Karpov was leading 5-3, without a winner being declared and under circumstances that have never been fully clarified to this day. In the second match, Kasparov led 12-11 before the final game. Karpov had to win to retain his title, but Kasparov won with black and took the match 13-11. At the age of 22, he became the youngest world champion in history at the time.

Garry Kasparov is world champion | Photo: Tass Archive

Before the final game of the World Championship match in Seville, challenger Karpov led world champion Kasparov 12-11. Kasparov had to win with white to defend his title. But instead of desperately trying to force a win and create tactical complications at all costs, Kasparov chose to keep Karpov under prolonged and sustained pressure in a complicated, slightly better position. The plan worked: while searching for a safe route to a draw, Karpov ran into time trouble and drifted into a lost position. After 64.Kg2 , he resigned and Kasparov remained world champion.

Vladimir Kramnik entered the World Championship match against Kasparov as the underdog, but he was well-prepared and ultimately won 8½-6½ - Kasparov failed to win a single game in 15. The diagram shows the decisive position from game two. Kramnik played 38.Rb6+ and after 38...Ke7? (after 38...Kg7 White is better, but not yet winning) 39.Bd5 , he won a piece and the game. The match also became famous for Kramnik's strategy of neutralising Kasparov's famously strong opening preparation with the Berlin Defence, which at the time was regarded as theoretically dubious.

Four years after winning the title, Kramnik struggled to defend it in his World Championship match against Peter Leko. Kramnik trailed by one point before the final game and absolutely had to beat the famously solid Leko in order to retain his title. And he managed it: in the diagrammed position, he transformed a better position into a winning one with 25.b6! . The match ended 7-7, and Kramnik remained world champion.

Two of the greatest players of all time suffer from chess blindness. World champion Magnus Carlsen played 26.Kd2? in this position and overlooked the relatively simple tactical trick 26...Nxe5, at least for a player of his level. After 27.Rxg8, Black has the intermediate check 27...Nxc4 and emerges with two extra pawns. But Viswanathan Anand also missed this opportunity - he lost the game and with it a good chance. Carlsen won the match 6½-4½ and defended the title he had taken from Anand in 2013.

Magnus Carlsen in 2014 | Photo: Ahmed Mukhtar, ChessBase India

The World Championship match between Carlsen and challenger Sergey Karjakin was tied 6-6 after 12 games. Carlsen won the rapid tiebreak 3-1 and ended the final game, and with it the World Championship match, with the spectacular queen sacrifice 50.Qh6+ . The game was played on 30 November, Carlsen's birthday.

The longest game in World Championship history: 136 moves, almost eight hours, an epic endgame - and in the end, once again, Carlsen won. After five draws, this was his first victory against challenger Ian Nepomniachtchi. Carlsen eventually won the match 7½-3½, and after this defeat very little went right for Nepomniachtchi.

After 14 classical games, the World Championship match between Ian Nepomniachtchi and Ding Liren was tied 7-7. In the fourth rapid game of the tiebreak, Ding avoided the perpetual check that was possible after 46...Kg8 and instead placed his rook in the dangerous-looking self-pin with 46...Rg6! , playing for the win. His willingness to take a risk was rewarded: Ding won the game and the tiebreak and became the first Chinese world champion. Nepomniachtchi and Ding were able to play for the title because Carlsen had declined to defend it.

Challenger Gukesh Dommaraju was considered the favourite in his match against world champion Ding Liren because Ding had appeared mentally fragile in the period before the match. But the match was only decided in the 14 th and final game, when Ding threw away a drawn endgame in one move with 55.Rf2? . Gukesh won the match 7½-6½ and, at the age of 18, became the youngest world champion in history.

title: AI Powered Opening Preparation
summary:
Working with the ChessBase ’27: what is a session with the new program like. In an example we show you what it looks like when a top player prepares against an opponent, what information the AI can derive, within seconds, from giant databases of millions of games.

Preparation with ChessBase ’27

Say you are facing a top player, and need to brush up on his strengths and weaknesses – you want to plan on what opening you will play against him. Of course you can extract his simply extract his games and start playing through them, getting an overview and reaching a decision. That can take hours. AI can offer some powerful assistance.

This is what a session with the ChessBase ’27 AI can look like. Remember, all of the material is extracted from the giant database within seconds. In the transcription below, "[=>game]" indicates a link the program gives to a game, which you can replay and analyse.

Your question: My next game is with black against Vincent Keymer. How do I prepare?

Click screen shot to enlarge

Answer: I wouldn't spend your preparation on the Caro-Kann Advance on your board. Keymer almost never plays 1.e4 against the Caro-Kann. As White he mostly opens with 1.Nf3 and 1.c4, and there's one specific line worth preparing.

1. What he plays as White (Mega 2026, games since 2023, blitz and online included)

- 1.Nf3: 779 games

- 1.d4: 533 games

- 1.c4: 284 games

- 1.e4: only 48 games, mostly against the Sicilian and Ruy Lopez

He has only 6 Caro-Kann games with white in the whole database. The recent ones are his 2025 Tata Steel wins against Praggnanandhaa [=>game] and a draw against Abdusattorov. The Advance Variation probably won't come up.

2. His main line: 1.Nf3 d5 2.e3

After 1.Nf3 d5 he plays 2.e3 in 228 games, far more than 2.g3 (48), 2.b3 (20), 2.c4 (18) or 2.d4 (17). Then 2...Nf6 3.c4 c6 4.Nc3 is his standard setup, with 113 games after 4.Nc3. Since you play the Caro-Kann, ...c6 with ...d5 is a natural fit for you. He also reaches it from 1.c4 c6, so one plan covers both his first moves.

3. The key position after 4.Nc3: two good replies

- 4...a6: this is where he scores badly. Of the newest 8 of his 18 games, he has +1 =1 -6. He lost to Caruana [=>game], Abdusattorov, So, Dardha and Le. These were mostly faster games, and it's only 8 games, but the trend is clear. Across all players the move scores 60% for White in 1,635 LiveBook games, so Black is in good shape. Black can follow up with ...b5 or ...Bf5/...Bg4 depending on what White does.

- 4...e6: the main move (3,523 LiveBook games, 61% for White). It's more solid, but Keymer wins often against it in blitz. His most important recent loss was here, though: the classical game Keymer–Abdusattorov, Tata Steel 2026 [=>game], a good model game for Black.

- I would avoid 4...g6 and 4...Bg4. They score 65% for White in the LiveBook, and his results against both are very good.

4. If he plays 1.d4 instead

Play your Slav: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6. He has 45 games there since 2023, including two draws against Erigaisi in 2025 [=>game]. That gives you a solid structure that goes with your Caro-Kann.

5. A sharper option: 2...c5

After 1.Nf3 d5 2.e3, the answer 2...c5 has beaten him several times: Wesley So twice in 2025 [=>game] and Vidit. It's worth knowing if you want a less symmetrical position.

Practical tips

- Keymer is very good at slow manoeuvring and gets a lot from quiet positions. Play for a solid structure and active pieces rather than for a fixed line of theory.

- He scores 66% with White overall. Treat an equal middlegame as a good result for you.

About the data: the database counts include many blitz and Titled Tuesday games, some games appear twice, and there's a different player named "Keymer, C" in it. Read the numbers as trends. You also don't have a Black repertoire set up yet, so I couldn't compare this with your own lines.

Next step: I could build a compact repertoire tree from the position after 4.Nc3 with 4...a6, with notes on the plans, and save it together with his model games in a new database.
